name: Pepper Water
subtitle: the thin black-peppery tamarind broth mulligatawny was built on, drunk over plain rice

ingredients.qty: 2 tbsp pulp, soaked in 200ml warm water

ingredients.note: gives just enough body; leave it out for a clearer broth
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in warm water for 15 minutes, then squeeze it out and strain. The fibres will ruin the texture otherwise.
Crush the pepper and cumin together coarsely in a mortar. Shop-bought pepper powder is too fine and tastes dusty.
If you are using the dal, boil and mash it before you start; it goes in at the end.

steps.text: Pound the black pepper, cumin seeds and 4 of the garlic cloves to a coarse, gritty paste.
steps.tip: Coarse is the point. A smooth paste makes the broth cloudy and the pepper stops crackling on the tongue.

steps.text: Bring the strained tamarind water, the remaining water, the chopped tomato, turmeric and salt to a boil in a wide pan.
Boil hard for 5 minutes until the raw, puckering smell of the tamarind has gone.
steps.tip: This step is not optional. Under-boiled tamarind tastes green and metallic.

steps.text: Stir in the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic paste and simmer 8 minutes.
If using, whisk the mashed toor dal with a ladle of the hot broth and stir it back in. Simmer 3 minutes more.
In a small pan heat the coconut oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dried red chillies, the remaining bruised garlic and the curry leaves.
steps.tip: Wait for the mustard to actually pop before the rest goes in, or the tempering tastes raw.

steps.text: Stir in the asafoetida off the heat for 5 seconds and pour the whole tempering into the pepper water.
Cover at once and let it stand 2 minutes so the aromatics steep, then scatter the coriander leaves.
Serve very hot, either in cups on its own or poured over plain rice with a spoon of ghee.

storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and the flavour deepens. Reheat only to a simmer; boiling it again dulls the pepper. Do not freeze.
